newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pilot probably conscious when he vanished.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pilot probably conscious when he vanished.

text.p: The pilot of a missing U.S. warplane appeared to be conscious and at the controls when it went far off course over Colorado but authorities still cannnot explain his actions, the Air Force said on Friday.
"I cannot say why he would have taken this action and unfortunately we may never know that answer," Maj. Gen. Donald Peterson told reporters.
"We don't think the airplane was on the autopilot; he was probably flying it," Peterson said. "But what his intentions were we couldn't say."
Heavy snow and overcast skies on Friday continued to hamper the search for the plane, concentrated in Colorado near the Vail ski resort.

Peterson said he would not speculate when asked about suggestions the pilot might have crashed the plane, an A-10, to commit suicide. On the contrary, he said, the pilot could have been lost with all navigation gauges dead.

Another Air Force official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said earlier there was no suicide note or other evidence that the pilot, Capt. Craig Button, 32, intended to kill himself when the plane vanished last week.
CNN quoted sources as saying Button appeared distraught after a recent meeting with his parents. It said his mother had joined the Jehovah's Witness religion.
"I wouldn't speculate on family affairs," Peterson said.

He said the pilot appeared to be flying the plane because it made at least half a dozen turns in the vicinity of the Aspen ski complex, and a backpacker said the plane came down through a hole in the clouds as if the pilot was looking for a landing spot.

But after refusing to speculate on whether the pilot might have been trying to commit suicide, Peterson also refused to speculate on whether he was looking for a landing spot, saying "I don't know the situation."
He said one of the best witness reports was by a group of cross-country skiers who heard a loud explosion and saw smoke south of the Vail ski resort.

The search is concentrated in that area, Peterson said, but snow has been so heavy and skies so overcast that searchers have not been able to cover it thoroughly, and they do not know precisely where the smoke was.

The plane was carrying four 500-pound (225 kg) practice bombs. Peterson said it was not clear from the skiers' description whether the explosion could have been the bombs going off or the plane crashing. He said the bombs almost certainly could not have exploded unless the pilot deliberately armed them.
The plane has been missing since April 2, when it disappeared as it was flying behind two other tank-attacking A-10s toward a bombing range near Gila Bend in southwest Arizona.

Spotty radar tracks of the plane combined with accounts by witnesses, including a group of schoolchildren in central Arizona, enabled Air Force coordinators to plot the plane's course to Colorado, where the eyewitness reports appeared to confirm that the plane had crashed, Peterson said.
When asked if there was any chance the pilot could still be alive, he said "Yes there is. We hope that's the case."
